$comment: P7-07: fictional visitors for the live practice check (pnpm eval:practice). Six scripted answers each, one per stage of the practice arc (opening, origin, belief, evidence, mistake, takeaway). 'vague' answers in generalities on purpose. Invented people; nothing here is anyone's real words.

answers: I help agencies of five to twenty people stop billing by the hour. Most of my clients raise their average project price by about 30 percent within two quarters.
My own agency went under in 2019. We billed hourly, said yes to every revision, and I worked out too late that our best clients were paying us least per hour.
Hourly billing punishes you for getting faster. The better your team gets, the less you earn, which is backwards.
One studio in Leeds moved twelve retainers to fixed project fees. Revenue went from 640 thousand to 910 thousand in a year with the same team of eight.
I once told a client to drop prices for a pitch they badly wanted. They won it and lost money on every month of the contract. Price to the value, not to the fear.
Charge for the outcome, not the hours.
I'm a sleep researcher. I help hospitals design rotas so night nurses get at least six hours of real sleep between shifts.
I worked nights as a porter at St Thomas' while doing my PhD, and I watched a colleague fall asleep at the wheel driving home after his fourth night in a row.
Forward-rotating shifts matter more than total hours. Going from days to evenings to nights is far easier on the body than the reverse.
In a trial across three wards, switching to forward rotation cut sick days by 22 percent over six months and reported errors fell by a third.
Early on I pushed for longer breaks during night shifts. Nobody took them because the wards were short-staffed. I learned to change the rota, not to ask for more of people.
Rotate shifts forward, never backward.
I help people become better leaders. It's about mindset and really understanding what leadership means.
I've always been interested in people and how teams work, and over the years I just developed a passion for it.
I think leadership is more about who you are than what you do. It's a journey, really.
I've seen lots of people grow a lot. When leaders get it, everything changes for the team.
There were times things didn't go as planned, but you learn from everything, and that's part of growth.
Be authentic and lead with purpose.
I run beginner courses at a climbing wall in Sheffield. Most of my students are over thirty-five and have never climbed before.
I started climbing at forty after a divorce. The instructors were all twenty-two and taught like I was too, and I nearly quit after week two.
Adults don't need more strength to start, they need permission to be bad at something in public.
We changed the first session to start on the easiest wall with no ropes, just traversing. Course completion went from 55 percent to 81 percent in a year.
I used to correct technique from the first climb. Students froze. Now I don't give a single tip until the third session.
Let beginners be beginners.
I do the books for about sixty tradespeople around Cardiff, mostly plumbers and electricians who hate paperwork.
My dad was an electrician who kept receipts in a biscuit tin. In 2015 he got a tax bill he couldn't pay because nobody had told him to put money aside.
Tradespeople don't have a tax problem, they have a cash flow problem that turns into a tax problem in January.
Clients who move 25 percent of every invoice into a separate account the day it's paid have had no late tax payments in four years. Not one.
I once filed a return for a client using his bank statements without checking his van finance. It cost him 1,800 pounds in missed allowances, and I paid it back.
Put a quarter of every payment away the day it lands.
